{{italic title}}
'''''The Book of Numbers''''' is a 1996 mathematics book by [[John Horton Conway|John H. Conway]] and [[Richard K. Guy]]. It discusses individual numbers, and types of number, that have proved conceptually significant. Topics include the origin of the nursery rhyme "[[Hickory Dickory Dock]]", [[figurate number]]s, the [[Fibonacci sequence]], [[transcendental number|transcendental]] numbers, the [[Metonic cycle]], [[combinatorics]], the [[complex number|complex plane]], [[nimber]]s, and [[surreal number]]s.<ref name="Bremner" /><ref name="Stenger" /><ref name="Brown" />

The Basic Library List Committee of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] has recommended that it be included in undergraduate mathematics libraries.<ref name="Stenger"/>

==Reception==
Andrew Bremner called the book "a delight" and opined that readers of [[Martin Gardner]] would appreciate it.<ref name="Bremner">{{Cite journal |last=Bremner |first=Andrew |date=1997 |title=none <!--deliberately chosen; do not fill in just for the sake of filling in--> |journal=The American Mathematical Monthly |volume=104 |issue=9 |pages=884–888 |jstor=2975310 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1997.11990734}}</ref> A. Robert Pargeter found it "fascinating" both for systematic reading and for browsing, and he recommended that school and college libraries carry it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pargeter |first=A. Robert |date=1998 |title=none |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |volume=82 |issue=493 |pages=147–148 |doi=10.2307/3620188 |jstor=3620188 }}</ref>

Sarah Gourlie called the book "organized and enlightening", while observing that some topics were considerably more demanding than others.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gourlie |first=Sarah |date=2005 |title=none |jstor=25678531 |journal=Math Horizons |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=26–27 |doi=10.1080/10724117.2005.12021805 }}</ref> Likewise, reviewing the book for the Mathematical Association of America, Allen Stenger noted that while the book only presumed knowledge of high-school [[algebra]] and [[trigonometry]], it also in places demanded a "high level of mathematical reasoning". Stenger expected that many readers would be unable to follow all of the explanations unaided.<ref name="Stenger">{{cite web |mode=cs1 |last=Stenger |first=Allen |date=2009-05-19 |title=The Book of Numbers |url=https://old.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/the-book-of-numbers |access-date=2025-02-09 |website=MAA Reviews |publisher=Mathematical Association of America}}</ref> A retrospective by [[Ezra Brown]] also commented on the "more than a little sophistication" required to follow some of Conway and Guy's discussions, while finding that the authors' joy "comes through on every page".<ref name="Brown">{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Ezra |date=2009 |title=A New Testament for the Book of Numbers |jstor=25678832 |journal=Math Horizons |volume=17 |issue=1 |page=29 |doi=10.1080/10724117.2009.11974841 }}</ref>

The [[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive]] quotes a review of this book in its biography of Conway, saying that "the publishers should have been required to post a warning label on the front cover indicating that this book contains extremely addictive material."<ref>{{MacTutor|id=Conway|title=John Horton Conway|mode=cs1}}</ref>
